blocks.title: What the numbers force
blocks.text: At ~23 Tbps average egress a ==CDN is mandatory==, and at 5000:1 the **read path** is designed first.

{blue:Control plane}: API servers handle metadata and ==signed URLs==
{orange:Data plane}: video bytes flow client to object store and CDN
Video bytes ==never pass through API servers==
Edge: **API gateway** (auth, rate limits) in front of the **upload service**
Storage: ==object store== for raw and encoded files, **metadata DB** for state
Processing: **transcode workers** fed by a queue

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Buy commodity infrastructure, build what differentiates. At 23 Tbps average egress, own CDN hardware starts to pay off; below that, rent.

blocks.title: Never proxy the bytes
blocks.text: Streaming uploads through API servers makes them a **bandwidth bottleneck** and gives no resumability. Use ==pre-signed multipart URLs==.
Video Streaming Platform: one raw upload goes in, a ladder of playable renditions comes out.

items: Convert one raw file into a ==ladder of renditions==
Plus ==audio tracks== and ==thumbnails==
Ladder example: 240p at 0.4 Mbps up to 4K at 16 Mbps (about 6 rungs)
Split into ==2-10 s GOP-aligned chunks== so each chunk starts on a keyframe
Encode chunks in ==parallel== on a worker fleet, run as a {blue:DAG of tasks}
A 1 h video finishes in ==minutes==, not hours
{purple:Per-title encoding}: ladder fitted to content complexity (Netflix), saves ~==20%== bitrate
{orange:AV1} saves ~30% vs H.264 but encodes ==5-10x slower==: popular titles only
Every chunk task is a row in ==transcode_jobs==; finished renditions are recorded in ==renditions==
Manifest path in `renditions` is what the player is later handed
Chunk tasks are ==idempotent==: same input, same output key, safe to rerun
==3 retries==, then the chunk goes to a ==dead-letter queue==
Spot-instance preemption just ==reruns the chunk==
A ==poison video== (crashes every worker) is quarantined, not retried forever

blocks.title: Mark READY last
blocks.text: Set `READY` only after ==all chunks== are packaged and manifests are written. A partly encoded ladder must never be playable.

items: ==Queue depth==: also the autoscale signal for the worker fleet
==Time-to-ready p95==: target under ==2x video duration==
==Cost per encoded minute==, tracked per codec
==Failure rate== and dead-letter queue size
==VMAF== quality score per rendition

blocks.text: 1. What ABR Is and What the Manifest Lists

items: ==ABR== = video cut into **2-6 s segments**, one set per bitrate
The player picks the **next segment's rendition** only, never the whole video
Inputs: ==measured throughput== and ==buffer level== (seconds of video queued)
{blue:HLS}: `.m3u8` playlists, master playlist → media playlist per rendition
{purple:DASH}: one XML `.mpd` file; both list renditions and segment URLs

blocks.note: HLS master playlist: one entry per rung, each points to a media playlist

items: {blue:Throughput-based}: ==EWMA== of the last few segment download speeds
{purple:Buffer-based (BBA)}: pick the rung from buffer seconds, ignore speed
{green:Hybrid}: buffer sets the safe zone, throughput picks inside it
Switch **down fast** (one bad segment), switch **up slowly** (several good ones)
Slow up-switching stops ==oscillation== between two rungs

steps.note: EWMA falls, player reacts at once
3.2 Mb in 3.2 s, 8 s buffer holds, no stall

items: ==CMAF fMP4== segments: one set serves both HLS and DASH
Only the manifests differ, so storage and cache footprint ==halve==
Segments too long (**10 s+**): slow switching, stalls before a down-switch
Segments too short: request overhead and low CDN efficiency
Keyframes not aligned across renditions: switch causes a glitch
Ladder with huge gaps between rungs: big quality jumps, oscillation

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: The player decides, not the server. Segments are **2-6 s** and **GOP-aligned** across every rung so switching is seamless: ==down fast, up slow==.
(Video Streaming Platform) 250 PB/day egress is about **23 Tbps** average, so the CDN carries the read path.

blocks.title: Why 480p does not stall
blocks.text: A 4 s segment at 0.8 Mbps is 3.2 Mb. On a 1 Mbps link it downloads in **3.2 s**, under 4 s, so the buffer still grows.

items: CDN edge hit ratio ==95%+==, so origin sees under 5% of 23 Tbps

blocks.q: The ladder is 240p 0.4, 360p 0.8, 480p 1.5, 720p 3 and 1080p 6 Mbps, with 4 s segments. Throughput falls from 4 Mbps to 1 Mbps while the buffer holds 8 s. Which rung should the next segment use, and what happens if the player picks 480p?
a_bullets: Pick ==360p==: it is the highest rung at or below 1 Mbps.
360p segment = 0.8 x 4 = 3.2 Mb, so it downloads in 3.2 s and the buffer grows by 0.8 s.
480p segment = 1.5 x 4 = 6 Mb, so it takes 6 s to download against 4 s of playback.
The buffer drains 2 s per segment, so it empties after about 4 segments and the player stalls.
Switch down fast: waiting to confirm the drop costs buffer.

blocks.q: A re-encoded rendition is written to the same path as before, /v/123/720p/seg5.m4s. Segments carry a 1-year TTL. Viewers keep seeing the old video. What is the bug and the fix?
a_bullets: Immutable caching assumes a path never changes content, so edges keep serving the old bytes for up to a year.
Fix: put a version or content hash in the path, such as /v/123/v2/720p/seg5.m4s.
The manifest has a short TTL and points to the new paths, so players move to the new segments.
Purging the CDN instead is slow and unreliable across POPs.

blocks.q: A new video goes viral and 200 POPs miss on the same segment within one second. How many origin fetches reach the object store?
a_bullets: Without coalescing, every viewer request that misses can reach origin, so thousands of fetches.
Edge request coalescing leaves 1 request per POP, so up to 200 origin fetches.
With an origin shield, the POPs' misses are collapsed into ==1 fetch==, assuming all POPs route through one shield.
If there is one shield per region, expect a few fetches, one per region.
The origin never sees the load, because the first fetch fills the shield and the rest are HITs.

blocks.q: The stream job shows 1,000,000 views for a video. The nightly batch over the raw log says 1,004,000. Which number is wrong, and is that a bug?
a_bullets: Neither is a bug: the display count is approximate and the batch count is the exact one.
Events arriving after the 5-minute watermark are dropped from the windowed count but stay in the raw log.
The batch job recomputes from the raw log, so it is the source of truth for payouts.
A drift of 0.4% is above the 0.1% target, so investigate lag or the watermark size, but do not bill from the stream.
